---
title: "Data Preparation and Cleaning in Excel"
---


::: {.learning-objectives}
## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Explain why accounting data must be prepared before it is analyzed, and document the preparation so that a reviewer can repeat it.
2. Use text functions to extract, standardize, and validate text fields, such as the product type encoded in an item code.
3. Use date functions to assign transactions to fiscal periods and to measure the time between business events.
4. Combine data from related tables with XLOOKUP, INDEX and MATCH, and VLOOKUP, and recognize when a one-to-many relationship calls for a different approach.
5. Build a repeatable preparation workflow in Power Query that merges tables, adds calculated columns, and can be refreshed when the source data changes.
:::


## Opening Scenario {.unnumbered}

The analysis workbook you built in Chapter 4 ended with a clue and an open question. The Furniture Seasonal Promotion carries more invoice lines and more discount dollars than any other promotion, and its effective dates, September and October 2026, straddle the two quarters whose margins the controller wants explained. When you tell her, she asks the obvious next question: how many of those discounted lines fell in the fourth quarter, and how much of the Furniture revenue did they account for? You cannot answer yet. The invoice lines record what was sold, at what price, and under which promotion, but not when the invoice was issued, which product group the item belongs to, or which customer bought it. That information lives in other Tables: the invoices, the items, the customers, and the sales orders. Before any of the analysis in the rest of Part II can begin, you have to bring it together, check that it came together correctly, and make the result easy to refresh. This chapter teaches you how.



## Why Data Preparation Comes First

Data preparation is the work of transforming data from the form in which it was recorded into a form that suits a particular analysis. A review of the field describes it as the process of discovering, cleaning, integrating, and restructuring data, and it names the activities involved: profiling the data, matching records across sources, mapping one structure onto another, transforming formats, and repairing values that are wrong (Fernandes et al., 2023). In the analytics workflow you met in Chapter 1, it is the third stage, after the question has been defined and the data has been obtained, and before any analysis begins.

For accountants, preparation is rarely optional. Transaction systems store data in the form that suits recording it, spread across related tables, as you saw in Chapter 3. An analysis needs a different form: one table in which every row carries all the attributes the question depends on. Auditors face the same problem with data they receive from clients. Lee et al. (2020) note that client data often arrives incomplete and in an unusable format, so that considerable time must be spent cleansing, transforming, standardizing, and validating it before it can be analyzed. The same concern runs through accounting education. In a review of published data analytics teaching cases, Raschke and Charron (2021) found that most cases focus on analysis and communication, and that few cover the steps that come before analysis, such as extraction and data preparation.

Preparation is also where many analytical errors begin. A lookup that silently fails, a date assigned to the wrong quarter, or a join that duplicates rows can change every number that follows, and none of these errors announces itself. That is why this chapter pairs every preparation technique with a check: a count of the rows that failed to match, a total that must agree with its source, or a test that a field has the form it should. The quality dimensions you studied in Chapter 2, accuracy, completeness, consistency, and timeliness, are the standard the checks apply. And because preparation involves many small decisions, it has to be documented, as you learned in Chapter 4, so that someone else can repeat it and reach the same result.

@fig-05-01 shows the destination of this chapter. By the end of Tutorial 5.3, your workbook will contain a single table, InvoiceLines, in which every invoice line carries its invoice date and fiscal period, its item's group and product type, and its customer's segment and region. The rest of Part II analyzes that table.

![From Related Tables to One Analytical Table.](/visuals/svg/fig-05-01-invoicelines-map.svg){#fig-05-01 fig-alt="A diagram of the preparation this chapter performs. Four Tables from the analysis workbook, SalesInvoiceLine, SalesInvoice, Item, and Customer, are connected by their keys: each invoice line carries a SalesInvoiceID and an ItemID, and each invoice carries a CustomerID. Arrows show the columns each Table contributes to a single InvoiceLines table: the line's own quantity, prices, discount, line total, and promotion; the invoice date and customer from SalesInvoice; the item group, item code, and standard cost from Item; and the segment and region from Customer. Columns calculated during preparation, the fiscal year, fiscal quarter, period label, product type, and a whole-quantity check, are shown as added columns."}


## Text Functions

Text fields carry more information than their appearance suggests. An item code, an invoice number, or an account name often encodes attributes, such as a category, a year, or a sequence, that are not stored anywhere else. Text functions let you extract those attributes, standardize text so that values that mean the same thing also look the same, and test that each value has the form it should. @tbl-05-01 summarizes the functions this chapter uses.

| Function | What it returns | Example with a Charles River value |
|---|---|---|
| `LEFT(text, n)` | The first n characters | `LEFT("FUR-DSK-0075",3)` returns `FUR` |
| `MID(text, start, n)` | n characters starting at a position | `MID("FUR-DSK-0075",5,3)` returns `DSK` |
| `RIGHT(text, n)` | The last n characters | `RIGHT("SI-2025-007947",6)` returns `007947` |
| `LEN(text)` | The number of characters | `LEN("FUR-DSK-0075")` returns 12 |
| `FIND(find, text)` | The position of one text inside another | `FIND("-","FUR-DSK-0075")` returns 4 |
| `TRIM(text)` | The text without leading, trailing, or repeated spaces | Removes stray spaces from an imported name |
| `CLEAN(text)` | The text without non-printing characters | Removes line breaks copied in from another system |
| `SUBSTITUTE(text, old, new)` | The text with one string replaced by another | Replaces "Street" with "St" to standardize addresses |
| `UPPER`, `LOWER`, `PROPER` | The text in capitals, lower case, or with each word capitalized | `UPPER("Smith Ltd")` returns `SMITH LTD` |
| `VALUE(text)` | The number that a text value represents | Converts `"007947"` to 7947 |

: Text functions used for data preparation {#tbl-05-01}

### Extracting Parts of a Text Value

Charles River's item codes follow a pattern. Every item the company sells has a code of three parts separated by hyphens: a three-letter group code, a three-letter product type code, and a four-digit number. FUR-DSK-0075 is a desk in the Furniture group, and FUR-SDB-0002 is a sideboard. The Item Table has an ItemGroup column, but no column for the product type, so the only way to analyze sales by product type, such as desks against sideboards, is to extract it from the code. Because the parts have a fixed length, the formula `=MID([@ItemCode],5,3)` returns the product type for every item: it takes three characters starting at the fifth. When the parts of a code vary in length, you can locate the separators with FIND and compute the positions instead, and Microsoft 365 adds TEXTBEFORE and TEXTAFTER, which return the text before or after a separator directly.

Invoice numbers encode information too. SI-2025-007947 contains a document prefix, a year, and a sequence number. The year in the number is assigned when the invoice is numbered, and in a well-controlled system it should agree with the year of the invoice date. Extracting it with `=MID([@InvoiceNumber],4,4)` and comparing it with the invoice date is a simple validity test, which you will apply in the exercises.

### Standardizing Text

Values that mean the same thing should look the same, or lookups, filters, and counts will treat them as different. TRIM removes spaces at the start and end of a value and reduces repeated spaces to one. CLEAN removes non-printing characters, such as line breaks, that are often copied in from other systems. SUBSTITUTE replaces one string with another, which is useful for standardizing abbreviations. UPPER, LOWER, and PROPER change the case of the letters.

Standardizing should be deliberate, because it can damage values that were already correct. PROPER capitalizes the first letter of every word and lowers the rest, so it turns a supplier named Donaldson LLC into Donaldson Llc and the connecting word in Watson, Mitchell and Chen into And. It also changes item names such as a sideboard "48 in" wide into "48 In". When a field is already consistent, the right preparation step is to leave it alone and record that you checked it.

### Validating Text

Before you clean a field, test whether it needs cleaning. The formula `=LEN([@CustomerName])=LEN(TRIM([@CustomerName]))` returns TRUE when a name has no stray spaces, and a COUNTIFS on the result tells you how many values fail. Applied to the Charles River names, codes, and addresses, tests like this find nothing to remove: the text fields are clean. That is a finding worth recording, not a wasted step. A preparation workflow that cleans data it has not tested can introduce errors, and one that tests and finds nothing has evidence that the field can be trusted. You can also test the form of a value, for example that every item code has twelve characters with hyphens in the fourth and eighth positions.

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
Some problems are invisible on screen. Text copied from a web page can contain a non-breaking space, character 160, which looks like an ordinary space but is not removed by TRIM. If a value that looks clean still fails to match, `=SUBSTITUTE(A2,CHAR(160)," ")` replaces non-breaking spaces with ordinary ones before TRIM runs. Numbers stored as text are another invisible problem: they look like numbers but do not add up, and they fail to match the same number stored as a number. VALUE converts them.
:::

## Date Functions

Accounting analysis is organized by period, so assigning each transaction to the right period is one of the most common preparation steps. Excel stores a date as a number of days, which is why dates can be subtracted and compared, and it provides functions that return the parts of a date. `YEAR`, `MONTH`, and `DAY` return the year, month, and day. `EOMONTH(date, 0)` returns the last day of the date's month, which is useful for month-end cutoff tests, and `EOMONTH(date, -1)+1` returns the first day.

### Assigning Fiscal Periods

Charles River's fiscal year is the calendar year, so the fiscal year of an invoice is `=YEAR([@InvoiceDate])` and its fiscal quarter is `=ROUNDUP(MONTH([@InvoiceDate])/3,0)`, which returns 1 for January through March and 4 for October through December. A period label such as 2026-Q4 is more useful than two separate numbers when you group, sort, and filter, and you can build one by joining text: `=[@FiscalYear]&"-Q"&[@FiscalQuarter]`.

Many organizations use a fiscal year that does not follow the calendar. For a fiscal year that begins in April, the formula `=INT(MOD(MONTH([@InvoiceDate])-4,12)/3)+1` returns quarter 1 for April through June and quarter 4 for January through March. The fiscal year itself then depends on the convention the organization uses to name it, typically the calendar year in which the fiscal year ends.

### Measuring Time Between Events

Subtracting one date from another returns the number of days between them. The formula `=[@DueDate]-[@InvoiceDate]` returns the payment terms of each invoice in days, and the difference between an invoice date and its order date measures how long an order took to be billed. For whole months or years between two dates, DATEDIF returns the difference in a chosen unit, as in `=DATEDIF(start, end, "m")`, although Excel does not suggest it as you type.

Measuring the age of a balance requires an as-of date. It is tempting to write `=TODAY()-[@InvoiceDate]`, but TODAY returns the date on which the workbook is opened, so the result changes every day and cannot be reproduced. A historical extract such as the Charles River data ends on a fixed date. Store the as-of date in a named parameter cell, as you did with the threshold in Chapter 4, and subtract from it instead.

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
A date that is stored as text looks like a date but behaves like text: it sorts alphabetically, it does not subtract, and it fails to match a real date. Text dates are common in data exported from other systems, especially when the export uses a different date order from your computer's settings. `DATEVALUE` converts a text date that Excel can recognize, and Power Query's data type setting, which you used in Chapter 4, converts a whole column. The Charles River workbook stores its dates as real dates, but always check the data type of a date column before you rely on it.
:::


## Lookup Functions

A lookup function retrieves a value from one table using a key from another. It is the spreadsheet equivalent of following a foreign key to the row it references, which you practiced by hand in Tutorial 3.2. Each invoice line carries a SalesInvoiceID, and the SalesInvoice Table holds exactly one row for each SalesInvoiceID, with its invoice date, customer, and totals. A lookup finds that row and returns the column you ask for, as @fig-05-04 shows.

![How XLOOKUP Retrieves a Value from Another Table.](/visuals/svg/fig-05-04-xlookup-anatomy.svg){#fig-05-04 fig-alt="A diagram of an XLOOKUP formula on real Charles River rows. On the left, an invoice line from the SalesInvoiceLine Table shows its SalesInvoiceID. On the right, rows of the SalesInvoice Table show SalesInvoiceID, InvoiceNumber, and InvoiceDate. Arrows show the three arguments of the formula: the lookup value is the line's SalesInvoiceID, the lookup array is the SalesInvoiceID column of SalesInvoice, where the matching row is highlighted, and the return array is the InvoiceDate column, from which the matching row's date is returned to the invoice line."}

### XLOOKUP

`XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found])` searches the lookup array for the lookup value and returns the value in the same position of the return array. To bring the invoice date onto each invoice line, the formula in a calculated column of the SalesInvoiceLine Table is:

```
=XLOOKUP([@SalesInvoiceID],SalesInvoice[SalesInvoiceID],SalesInvoice[InvoiceDate],"No match")
```

The fourth argument is the value returned when the key is not found. Without it, XLOOKUP returns the error #N/A. A text value such as "No match" is easier to count, and counting it is the first check on any lookup: a clean lookup has no unmatched rows.

### INDEX and MATCH, and VLOOKUP

Before XLOOKUP was added to Excel, the same retrieval was written by combining two functions. `MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_array, 0)` returns the position of the key in a column, and `INDEX(return_array, position)` returns the value at that position. Together, `=INDEX(SalesInvoice[InvoiceDate],MATCH([@SalesInvoiceID],SalesInvoice[SalesInvoiceID],0))` does what the XLOOKUP formula above does. The final 0 in MATCH asks for an exact match, which is almost always what accounting keys require. INDEX and MATCH work in every version of Excel, which matters when you share a workbook with someone who does not have Microsoft 365 or Excel 2021 or later.

VLOOKUP is the oldest of the three and the most limited. It searches only the first column of a range and returns a column identified by its number, as in `=VLOOKUP(key, range, 3, FALSE)`. Because the key must be in the leftmost column, it cannot look to the left, and because the return column is a number, the formula can return the wrong column if columns are added or removed. You will meet it in older workbooks, and it is worth recognizing, but XLOOKUP is the better choice for new work. @tbl-05-03 compares the three.

| Feature | VLOOKUP | INDEX and MATCH | XLOOKUP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Where the key can be | Only in the first column of the range | In any column | In any column |
| How the return column is chosen | By its number in the range | By reference to the column | By reference to the column |
| Effect of inserting or deleting columns | Can return the wrong column | None | None |
| Default match | Approximate, unless the last argument is FALSE | Exact when the last argument is 0 | Exact |
| When the key is not found | #N/A | #N/A | #N/A, or a value you supply |
| Availability | All versions of Excel | All versions of Excel | Microsoft 365 and Excel 2021 or later |

: Lookup functions compared {#tbl-05-03}

### Lookups Across Several Tables

Some attributes are two keys away. An invoice line does not carry a sales order key, but its invoice does. To find the date on which a line was ordered, first bring the invoice's SalesOrderID onto the line with one lookup, and then use that SalesOrderID to look up the order date in the SalesOrder Table with a second. Keeping each step in its own column makes the chain easy to check.

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
A lookup returns one value, the first match it finds. That is correct when the lookup follows a relationship toward its "one" side, from an invoice line to its invoice or from an invoice to its customer, because the key appears exactly once. It is wrong when it follows a relationship toward the "many" side. A sales order can have several shipments, so a lookup of an order's shipment date returns the date of whichever shipment comes first in the Table, not necessarily the earliest one. When the relationship is one-to-many, summarize instead: MINIFS returns the earliest shipment date, as in Tutorial 2.1, and SUMIFS or COUNTIFS return totals and counts. Chapter 3's discussion of cardinality tells you which side of a relationship you are on.
:::

::: {.callout-note .connecting-dots icon=false}
## Connecting the Dots
Every lookup in this chapter follows a foreign key to a primary key, the relationship you studied in Chapter 3. The same operation is called a join in SQL, where it is written in a query rather than in a column formula, and it is called a relationship in Power BI's data model. The skill of asking which key connects two tables, and on which side of the relationship each table sits, carries over to both of the tools you will learn in Parts III and IV.
:::

## Missing, Meaningful, and Invalid Values

Chapter 2 introduced missing values and duplicate records as data quality problems. Preparation adds a practical distinction: a blank cell does not always mean that information is missing. In the Charles River invoice lines, a blank PromotionID means that the line carried no promotion, and a blank ShipmentLineID on a design-service line means that nothing was shipped. These are meaningful blanks. They record a fact, and replacing them or treating them as errors would be wrong. A blank TrackingNumber on a shipment, as you found in Tutorial 2.1, is different: the information should exist and does not. Before you fill, remove, or flag blanks, decide which kind they are, and record the decision.

Formulas complicate the test for blanks. `ISBLANK` returns TRUE only for a cell that contains nothing at all, so it returns FALSE for a cell whose formula returns an empty text value, even though the cell looks empty. To find the rows a lookup failed to match, count the value you told the lookup to return, such as "No match", rather than testing for blanks.

A value can also be present and still be invalid for its purpose. A validity test checks that each value has the form or range it should. Charles River sells most items by the unit, recorded in the Item Table's UnitOfMeasure column as Each, so you might expect every quantity for those items to be a whole number. The test `=[@Quantity]<>INT([@Quantity])`, which returns TRUE for a quantity with a fractional part, finds that most invoice lines for items sold by the unit carry fractional quantities, such as the 3.74 sideboards billed on invoice line 10646. In practice, a finding like this goes to the owners of the source system with a question, because the cause could be a partial-unit shipping practice, a unit-of-measure setting, or an error in how quantities are recorded. For the analysis, what matters is whether the finding changes the answer. Revenue, list amounts, and discounts are recorded on each line and are consistent with one another, and an average price calculated as revenue divided by quantity is consistent across periods. Record the finding in the documentation as a known limitation of the quantity data, and avoid conclusions that depend on whole units.

Duplicates are the last familiar problem. Excel's Remove Duplicates command, on the Data tab, deletes rows that repeat the values of the columns you choose. Use it with care: it deletes without asking which row to keep, and two rows that look the same may record two genuine transactions. As in Chapter 2, count and examine suspected duplicates before removing anything, and remove them in a query or a copy, never in the source data.


## Power Query for Repeatable Preparation

The lookup columns you add in Tutorial 5.2 work, but they have two weaknesses for a lasting analysis. They live as formulas in the loaded Table, so every refresh recalculates thousands of lookups, and the preparation they perform is spread across several columns rather than recorded as a single procedure. Power Query, which you used in Chapter 4 to import the data, can perform the same preparation as a recorded sequence of steps that runs whenever the data is refreshed.

### Merging Queries

Power Query's equivalent of a lookup is a merge. Merge Queries, on the Home tab of the Power Query Editor, combines two queries by matching a key column in each, and adds the matching rows of the second query as a new column that you then expand into the columns you need. A merge has a join kind, which decides which rows appear in the result. @tbl-05-04 lists the join kinds you will use most.

| Join kind | Rows in the result | Accounting use |
|---|---|---|
| Left outer | Every row of the first query, with the matching rows of the second | Adding invoice and item details to every invoice line |
| Inner | Only the rows that match in both queries | Keeping only lines whose item appears in a filtered item list |
| Full outer | Every row of both queries, matched where possible | Comparing two lists, such as a subledger and a ledger extract |
| Left anti | Only the rows of the first query that have no match in the second | Finding orphaned records, such as lines whose item is missing |

: Join kinds in Power Query merges {#tbl-05-04}

For enriching the invoice lines, left outer is the right choice, because every invoice line must stay in the result whether or not its match is found. A left anti merge on the same keys is a useful check: it returns the lines that failed to match, which should be none. Because every key in the Charles River invoice lines refers to a single row in the table it references, a left outer merge returns exactly as many rows as the invoice lines query started with, and checking that the row count has not changed is the first test of any merge.

### Custom Columns

A custom column, added through Add Column > Custom Column, calculates a new column with a formula written in Power Query's formula language, called M. The functions differ from Excel's, but the ideas are the same. `Date.Year([InvoiceDate])` returns the year, `Date.QuarterOfYear([InvoiceDate])` returns the quarter, and `Text.Middle([ItemCode], 4, 3)` returns three characters of the item code starting after the fourth. Note that Text.Middle counts positions from zero, where Excel's MID counts from one, so the same product type code starts at position 4 in M and position 5 in Excel. As in Chapter 4, every custom column appears in the Applied Steps list, so the query records exactly how each value was calculated.

### Reference Queries and Refresh

A merge can change the query it is applied to, so it is good practice to build the combined table in a new query rather than altering the queries that load the source Tables. Right-clicking a query in the Queries pane and choosing Reference creates a new query that starts from the result of the first one. The original query is unchanged, and the new query updates whenever the original does. When the data is refreshed, Power Query runs the source queries and then every step of the combined query, so the combined table is rebuilt from the current data without any formula being copied down.

::: {.callout-tip .in-practice icon=false}
## In Practice
Junior auditors are routinely asked to prepare client data for testing. In a teaching case built around that task, Hunter et al. (2020) describe cleaning large data sets as a vital task that is routinely performed by the most junior member of the audit team, and they pair the cleaning with checks that the prepared data is complete and accurate. A preparation workflow that records its steps, reconciles its row counts and totals to the source, and can be rerun on the next extract is exactly the evidence such checks require.
:::

## Looking Ahead

This chapter has prepared the Charles River invoice lines for analysis. You have used text functions to extract a product type from an item code and learned when standardizing text helps and when it harms. You have assigned invoices to fiscal periods, measured the time between orders and invoices, and seen why an as-of date is better than TODAY. You have combined Tables with lookups, followed a key through two tables, and learned to count the rows a lookup failed to match. You have distinguished meaningful blanks from missing information and recorded a validity finding about quantities. Finally, you have built the same enrichment in Power Query as a refreshable InvoiceLines table and reconciled it with your lookups and with the source.

The preparation has already sharpened the controller's question. The Furniture Seasonal Promotion priced orders placed in September and October, but many of those orders were invoiced after the promotion ended, so its effect reaches further into the fourth quarter than its dates suggest. InvoiceLines now holds, for every invoice line, the period, the product group and type, and the customer segment that an answer requires. The remaining chapters of Part II analyze that table.
